entries.title: A geography of hearts: Turkiye and Lebanon, building the Levant together
entries.summary: Turkiye and Lebanon can build a stronger Levant through partnership, sovereignty and mutual respect.
entries.content:
Some journeys feel less like a first visit and more like a homecoming. That is how I felt during my three days in Lebanon — my first ever visit to a country I had long known through its history, its poets and its people, but had never walked through myself.

I came at the kind invitation of Dr Tarek Mitri, Deputy Prime Minister of Lebanon, who proved the most gracious of hosts. I came in a spirit of friendship and partnership, and I leave with gratitude. In every conversation — in Beirut, in Tripoli, in Akkar and beyond — I heard the same quiet determination: Lebanon wants to stand on its own feet, and it wants partners, not patrons.

I also leave with a full heart and, I must admit, a fuller stomach. From a za’atar breakfast on the road to Akkar to the sweets of Hallab in Tripoli and shawarma at Barbar in Beirut, Lebanese hospitality is everything people promise. Around shared tables, over strong coffee and long conversations, I was reminded that the bonds between our peoples were never only about diplomacy. Distance on a map tells you very little. What matters is the geography of hearts — and by that measure, Beirut and Istanbul have always been neighbours.

That warmth carries a responsibility, for friendship is proved not in words but in what we do together. Five convictions stayed with me throughout the visit.

1. Unity is Lebanon’s greatest strength

Lebanon’s diversity of faiths, communities and traditions is not a weakness to be managed; it is a richness to be protected. I was honoured to meet leaders from across the country’s political and spiritual life: President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and the veteran Speaker of Parliament, Nabih Berri; the Grand Mufti of the Lebanese Republic, Sheikh Abdul Latif Derian, and the Greek Orthodox Metropolitan of Beirut, His Eminence Elias Audi; Mrs Bahia Hariri, Vice President of the Future Movement; and Mr Walid Jumblatt, former leader of the Progressive Socialist Party. Different as their paths have been, each spoke of the same hope: a state that serves all its citizens, institutions that work and a future their children will not have to leave the country to find. National unity is the foundation on which everything else — security, recovery, prosperity — must be built. Turkiye’s interest is in a strong, whole and united Lebanon.

2. Lebanon’s decisions belong to the Lebanese

For too long, Lebanon has paid the price of being treated as an arena for the rivalries of others. That has to end. Nowhere is this felt more deeply than in the south, whose towns, farmland and families have borne the heaviest cost of this year’s war. Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity are not negotiable — and they must extend to every inch of its land. Occupation in the south must end, and the Lebanese state must be able to protect all of its citizens, from Beirut to the southern border. The choices about Lebanon’s future must be made in Beirut, by Lebanese, for Lebanese. Foreign states — near or far — should respect that. Real friends offer support when it is asked for and step back when it is not. That is the principle Turkiye seeks to live by.

3. A Levant-driven future, built on trade

The problems of our region will not be solved one capital at a time, and they will not be solved from outside. The Levant must think and act as a region, as it once did. The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus records that the Phoenician cities held their common council in Tripoli, gathering there to deliberate on matters of the greatest importance. More than 2,000 years later, our region urgently needs to recover that tradition of meeting, talking and deciding together, and Tripoli, which welcomed me so warmly, is a fitting place to begin. Our economies are natural complements: Lebanon’s entrepreneurial talent, its banking and services heritage and its ports; Turkiye’s manufacturing base, logistics networks and access to Europe and Central Asia. As Syria recovers, a corridor of trade, transport and energy linking our countries can become the backbone of a new regional economy. Let goods, investment and young people’s ideas move freely across our region, and stability will follow prosperity.

4. A record, not a promise

Turkiye does not come to Lebanon with new slogans; we come with a track record. We have stood behind UNIFIL’s peacekeeping mission in the south. Through TİKA and the Turkish Red Crescent, we have delivered humanitarian aid in Lebanon’s hardest hours. Now the task is to rebuild the south — its homes and schools, its hospitals and roads and its olive groves — so that every displaced family can return home with dignity. Turkiye stands ready to play its full part in that effort, and to help strengthen the Lebanese institutions that must lead it. We have consistently defended Lebanon’s sovereignty in every international forum, and we will continue to do so. Through the foundations and educational institutions I work with, we have seen firsthand how much Lebanese students and young people have to offer — and how much our two societies gain when they learn side by side.

5. Interdependence is not dependence

In a fragile world, no country prospers alone. Cooperation between Turkiye and Lebanon is not charity flowing in one direction; it is interdependence that strengthens both. When Lebanon is stable, Turkiye and the whole region are safer. When Lebanese businesses grow, Turkish businesses gain partners. When our universities, civil society and young people connect, both nations gain. The goal is a partnership of equals — one where each side brings its strengths and neither loses its independence.

The road ahead

I leave Lebanon convinced that the moment for deeper partnership is now. Lebanon has endured more than its share of war, economic hardship and loss — especially this year, and the south most of all. Yet what I saw was not a country defeated but a people ready to rebuild. Turkiye will be there — not as a distant benefactor, but as a neighbour in the geography of hearts — until the last family has returned to its village in the south and the last school has reopened its doors. I hope this was the first of many visits, and that the friendships begun over these three days grow into lasting partnerships between our institutions, our businesses and, above all, our young people.

Shukran, Lebanon. Tesekkurler. Until we meet again.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

entries.title: Somalia expels UAE ambassador, accuses Abu Dhabi of violating sovereignty
entries.summary: Somalia says the UAE is interfering in its internal affairs with actions that amount to an 'open invasion'.
entries.content:
Somalia says the UAE is interfering in its internal affairs with actions that amount to an ‘open invasion’.

Somalia has ordered the United Arab Emirates (UAE) ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and withdrew its envoy from Abu Dhabi.

Announcing the measures on Thursday, Somali officials accused the UAE of violations of Somalia’s sovereignty that amounted to an “open invasion”.

“Measures will be taken against ‌anyone who cooperates with UAE in the invasion against Somalia,” Information Minister Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud said in a broadcast on the state-run news agency.

“All Somalis are urged to defend their country and unite against the open invasion of the UAE against the sovereignty, security, land and unity of Somalis,” he said.

Mohamud did not provide additional information on what provoked the expulsion.

There was no immediate response from the UAE foreign ministry.

On Tuesday, Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the UAE of giving economic and political support to regional Somali governments to oppose the federal government.

According to the Somalia National News Agency, Mohamud said Abu Dhabi signed agreements related to the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo with regional administrations and without the Federal Government.

He also said that the UAE helped to establish military bases and forces outside Somalia’s national command while the army is fighting the al-Shabab armed group and had given political and financial support that fuelled disputes inside the country.

The UAE, which has helped fund and train Somalia’s military in the past and has backed ports and other commercial ventures there, has long denied meddling in the country’s affairs.

Rising tensions

Expelling the UAE ambassador is the strongest measure Mogadishu has taken against Abu Dhabi since it annulled every agreement with the gulf state earlier this year.

In January, Somalia cancelled all agreements with the UAE, including port deals and defence and security ‌cooperation, ⁠citing “harmful actions” that undermine the country’s unity and sovereignty.

The UAE has long leveraged its wealth to expand its influence across the Horn of Africa, using a mix of economic, military and diplomatic clout to assert ⁠regional power.

The UAE trained ⁠hundreds of Somali troops from 2014 to 2018, and still pays salaries and provides logistics for around 3,400 Somali military police and special forces troops in and around the capital, according ⁠to senior Somali sources.

entries.title: What the ICJ genocide ruling means for the Rohingya people
entries.summary: This is the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.
entries.content:
This is the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya minority ethnic group.

After seven years of deliberations, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa delivered the long-awaited ruling on Thursday in a verdict which took three hours to read out.

Nine of the 15-judge panel found that Myanmar has committed genocide, the court said. Justices also voted in favour of a landmark reparations order against the country which it says has persecuted the mostly Muslim group for decades.

It is the first time in the history of the World Court, which was established in 1945, that it has ruled that a state has committed genocide. The decision is final and cannot be appealed.

The Gambia brought the landmark case against Myanmar in 2019.

After many years of persecution, Myanmar’s military launched an offensive in 2017 which forced about 750,000 Rohingya from their homes and lands, and pushed them into squalid refugee camps, largely in neighbouring Bangladesh.

About 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the early stages of the military operation. Thousands of others died in shipwrecks as they fled on perilous boat trips across the Bay of Bengal. The Rohingya reported cases of mass killings, torture and rape at the hands of the Myanmar military and allied militias.

“This is a huge day for the Rohingya people and all people of Myanmar,” said Matthew Smith, a campaigner with the advocacy group Fortify Rights, who nervously stood in The Hague’s Peace Palace along with Rohingya survivors and the Gambian delegation, as the ruling was read out.

“People have waited for such a long time for this moment,” he said.

The ruling “will provide much-needed momentum to efforts to hold the perpetrators and architects of the genocide individually criminally accountable”, he added.

Here’s what we know:

What has the court ruled?

The lengthy ruling, delivered by ICJ judge Yuji Iwasawa of Japan, said that Myanmar’s security forces “killed thousands of Rohingya” in Rakhine State, committed widespread sexual violence against them as well as acts of “extreme violence against children”.

Villages were “systematically destroyed”, replaced with permanent structures and then re-settled by non-Rohingya, the ruling said. The military also “intentionally” caused “serious bodily and mental harm” to the group’s members, and high-ranking officials disseminated anti-Rohingya hate speeches that portrayed them as “subhuman and a violent threat”.

Those who fled their homes have had little or no opportunity to return because of the destruction of their homes, the court found, and acts against children in particular established the military’s intent to “prevent birth” in the group.

Furthermore, the Myanmar military knew that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians and allied militias participated in the military campaign against the Rohingya. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” Iwasawa said.

The ICJ ruled that Myanmar must cease all acts of violence and investigate those culpable. Myanmar must also take immediate and effective steps to investigate all persons suspected of culpability, prosecute and punish the guilty, and provide guarantees that this will never happen again.

Importantly, the court ruled that Myanmar must institute restitution and reparations in the case – something campaigners have long pushed for.

Restitution measures, the court said, should see Myanmar: allow and facilitate the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; return or replace all collective property damaged; facilitate the search for the disappeared and ensure proper burials; provide for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured and ensure their protection from persecution.

The court said it could not determine compensation but ordered Myanmar to submit a report within two years outlining a plan.

“This judgement is a landmark victory for the Rohingya people and for countless individuals in Myanmar who have endured violence at the hands of the military. It represents an important step toward accountability and honours the courage and perseverance of the victims and survivors who have spent years seeking justice,” Arsalan Suleman, partner at legal firm Foley Hoag and lead counsel for The Gambia, said after the verdict was delivered.

For the Rohingya people, this is the day they have long hoped for.

“The Rohingya hope to receive justice and enjoy safety both inside and outside Myanmar,” Kyaw Min Sabber, founder of Rohingya Human Rights Initiative, told Al Jazeera ahead of the ruling.

“They also hope that they will no longer face displacement and arbitrary killings in Rakhine State,” he said.

Can the ICJ compel Myanmar to comply with this ruling?

The ICJ cannot enforce its rulings, but they do carry weight: The Gambia could now table the case at the United Nations Security Council and request action.

This ruling is especially significant because the 1948 Genocide Convention requires proof of the specific intent to destroy – in whole or in part – a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. That requirement is notoriously difficult to prove, and has contributed to the ICJ never having held a state responsible for committing genocide.

In 2007, for example, the court ruled that Serbia violated the Convention by failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops in Srebrenica but that the state itself did not commit the act – even though UN tribunals found individuals culpable for genocide.

Thursday’s ruling could, therefore, have important implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza.

Who are the Rohingya?

The Rohingya are a largely Muslim ethnic group based primarily in Myanmar’s western Rakhine State, which shares a border with Bangladesh.

Until their forced displacement in 2017, there were about 1.4 million Rohingya in Myanmar, making them a minority among Myanmar’s 137 ethnic groups. Other Rohingya populations live in India, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.

While the Rohingya identify as Indigenous to Myanmar – and have been present there for many generations – the government does not recognise them and maintains they are “illegal migrants” from Bangladesh. In 1982, authorities passed a citizenship law that essentially rendered most of the group’s population stateless. Successive governments, including the civilian-led administration of Aung San Suu Kyi that governed between 2016 and 2021, have continued to exclude the Rohingya.

The group has experienced waves of violence and displacement over the years. In 2013, the rebel Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) was formed. In late 2017, when ARSA attacked police posts, Myanmar’s armed forces, known as the Tatmadaw, launched a massive response operation. The Rohingya were subjected to unprecedented levels of violence: The military shot men dead, raped women, threw babies into fires and razed Rohingya villages, survivors said.

A UN fact-finding mission in 2019 concluded that the Tatmadaw gang-raped men, women and children, and committed “genocidal acts”.

The violence saw at least 740,000 Rohingya flee to Bangladesh in a span of months. About 1.2 million Rohingya now live in crowded conditions in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar, while about 520,000 remain in Myanmar under severe restrictions. Bangladesh wants them to return to Myanmar, and over the years, aid allocated for the Rohingya has shrunk, especially since United States President Donald Trump took office in January 2025 and slashed foreign aid spending.

What did The Gambia argue?

In November 2019, the small West African nation of The Gambia took Myanmar to The Hague. The Gambia, itself a Muslim-majority country, was backed by the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and was itself just emerging from years of repression under the dictator Yahya Jammeh.

Its team of lawyers, led by then-Justice Minister Aboubacarr Tambadou, argued that Myanmar had committed genocide in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

Former leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi, who was later overthrown in a military coup in 2021, personally appeared at the court at the time and called The Gambia’s claims “incomplete and misleading”.

But in January 2020, the ICJ ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent a genocide of Rohingya, in what experts called a “stunning rebuke” to Suu Kyi.

Eleven countries – Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, the Maldives, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Slovenia, Ireland, Belgium, France and Britain – applied to support the case.

During hearing in January 2026, The Gambia, led by current Justice Minister Dawda A Jallow, reiterated that Myanmar’s ruling military “deliberately targeted” the Rohingya for “destruction” and that it acted with “genocidal intent”.

The Gambia asked the court to establish Myanmar’s obligation to provide reparations to Rohingya survivors, order its government to prosecute those responsible, and ensure the Rohingya can return safely.

Myanmar – now under military leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the crackdowns and later took power in the 2021 coup – denied the allegations, however, arguing that its military was forced to respond to armed attacks with its “clearance operations”.

What does the ruling mean for Rohingya?

Survivors and rights groups say the ruling is clear vindication after decades of suffering.

The verdict also provides legal backing for justice and accountability at the highest level that could see the Rohingya achieve their goal of returning safely and with dignity to their homes, and of being finally acknowledged by the state of Myanmar.

Smith said the statement on reparations is especially important and that the court’s ruling now gives the parties ground to negotiate the details.

“Reparations for the Rohingya must be comprehensive, meaningful, and shaped by Rohingya survivors themselves,” he said, adding that it must not be conflated with aid or humanitarian assistance and must come with official acknowledgement of wrongdoing.

The plan should include financial compensation for the immense losses suffered, restitution of confiscated land and property, restoration of citizenship and fundamental rights, and guarantees of safe return, medical care, trauma support, education, and livelihood opportunities, he said.

“No amount of money can undo a genocide, but meaningful reparations can help restore rights, dignity, and a measure of justice to people who have been denied all three for generations,” Smith added.

Can the Rohingya return safely to Myanmar?

This is very uncertain. Myanmar is in turmoil, prompting serious concerns about their safety there.

The overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in 2021 triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and has displaced more than 3.5 million.

Fighting between the army and the Arakan Army, a largely Buddhist rebel group also operating in the Rakhine State which also targets the Rohingya, has worsened conditions further.

In August, Myanmar said it had verified more than 300,000 refugees in Bangladesh and registered them for repatriation, but stated that this could only begin after security is restored in Rakhine.

Furthermore, while a genocide finding formally recognises the harm the Rohingya have suffered, it may do little for them in the short term, Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer, told Al Jazeera ahead of the ruling.

“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” he said.

What happens next?

All eyes are now on whether – or how – Myanmar will implement the ICJ’s rulings and submit the required report by its November 2028 deadline.

Survivors want states which support the Rohingya to keep up pressure on Myanmar’s military to ensure an end to ongoing rights violations by the army and the Arakan Army, Kyaw Min Sabber said.

The Gambia, the OIC, and all the countries which have supported the case “have an important responsibility to continue supporting the protection and pursuit of justice for the Rohingya people”, he said, including those refugees living in India, Malaysia, Thailand, Nepal and other countries where they face mistreatment, arbitrary detention, and the fear of deportation.

“Their commitment should extend beyond the court proceedings and continue until the Rohingya can safely return to Myanmar with full equal rights, security, and dignity,” he said.

entries.title: ‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide – Cost of War
entries.summary: The trauma Israeli soldiers bring home — and the consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
entries.content:
Al Jazeera Originals

‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide – Cost of War

What happens when Israeli soldiers return from Gaza?

The film ‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide examines the psychological consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza through personal accounts of injury, grief and trauma by Israeli soldiers, alongside interviews with psychologists, journalists and Palestinian trauma specialists.

The film looks at the violence inflicted on Palestinians and asks how its consequences reach into Israeli families and society. Soldiers’ accounts of sleeplessness and fear sit alongside questions about military mental healthcare and the lasting effects of prolonged war.

Watch ‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide, part of Cost of War, from Al Jazeera Originals.

Published On 19 Nov 2026

entries.title: Canada’s beloved Tim Hortons brews ire over ‘excessive’ Israeli data deal
entries.summary: Advocates raised concerns about consumer privacy and data-sharing, involving a firm with ties to Israel's military.
entries.content:
Advocates raised concerns about consumer privacy and data-sharing, involving a firm with ties to Israel’s military.

When Canadians order their morning cup of joe using the coffeehouse chain Tim Hortons app, coffee may not be the only thing being delivered. Users’ sensitive personal data could also be travelling across the world – to an Israeli cybertech company.

The beloved nationwide chain has found itself at the centre of an angry backlash over consumer privacy and its ties to Forter, the Israeli firm.

On Tuesday, Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CPJME) revealed that the Tim Hortons app has been sending “sensitive user data” to Forter. Al Jazeera has independently confirmed that the app does share user data with Forter.

CPJME also raised concerns about Forter’s founders’ links to an Israeli military intelligence unit accused of mass surveillance of Palestinians, as well as the unit’s reported association with Lavender, an artificial intelligence (AI) system used to generate lists of Palestinians to be targeted during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

The group’s findings build on an investigation by Canadian broadcaster CBC reported last week, examining the data-sharing practices of some of the country’s most popular apps. But the investigation did not identify which company was receiving Tim Hortons users’ data or disclose where it was based.

Neither Tim Hortons nor its parent company, Restaurant Brands International (RBI), had responded to Al Jazeera’s queries by the time of publication. Forter had also not responded to Al Jazeera’s queries.

Tim Hortons told CBC that the data-sharing arrangement is a fraud-prevention measure. However, experts have described the extent of the data collected as overly intrusive.

“The collection occurs prior to consent, and in my view is excessive,” Joel Reardon, a computer science professor at the University of Calgary whose research underpinned the CBC investigation, told Al Jazeera.

CPJME, meanwhile, warned that the practice could expose consumers to privacy risks that extend far beyond the original purpose of fraud prevention.

“What concerns us is that there is this massive … digital footprint being built of people through these apps, seemingly without their knowledge, in the name of preventing fraud, and that data is flowing to an Israeli cybertech company whose operations … [are] opaque to us and [who] have concerning ties,” Jason Toney, CJPME’s director of media advocacy, told Al Jazeera.

From doughnuts to digital footprint

During its investigation, CBC found that the apps it examined, including Tim Hortons’, disclose that they collect or share certain data. However, experts questioned whether the amount of information gathered was proportionate to the simple act of buying a cup of coffee.

CBC found that the app appeared to send data to the third-party company right when it launches. This data includes unique identifiers, sensor details and the names of nearby Wi-Fi networks, which Reardon said can be used to determine a person’s location.

“I’m usually troubled by the precise ongoing location data collection because that can reveal a great deal of information about an individual,” said Reardon.

He explained that Forter gathers enough information from the Tim Hortons app to create a digital fingerprint for each device, so it can be identified in the future.

That is concerning for OpenMedia, a Canadian organisation advocating for digital rights, privacy and consumer protection.

“People open the Tim Hortons app to order a coffee, not have their data, including location indicators, exported to foreign companies,” its executive director, Matt Hatfield, told Al Jazeera.

But he said Tim Hortons is not unusual in doing this. “Many companies quietly pass data to a long chain of vendors that customers have never heard of and never chose.”

“We effectively create these chains of trust that our data is handled appropriately – where any company along the chain can breach and abuse our data,” Hatfield said.

Tim Hortons told CBC that the third party it works with – Forter – is not allowed to sell the data it collects through its app and that the coffee chain itself does not sell users’ personal information.

But Reardon said effective fraud prevention can be carried out without collecting data giving users’ precise locations.

“It is useful to be clear if Tim Hortons is talking about protecting [themselves] from fraud, or if they [are] protecting the users,” the researcher added.

Forter’s founders have previously told media that the data it receives is used to protect “wealthy corporations” from fraudulent activity, Toney noted. “If a consumer’s credit card is fraudulently used, for example, to purchase something online, it’s usually the wealthy corporations that are on the hook for reimbursing that funding,” he explained.

“So they use Forter to avoid having to take on those costs … It’s not really about protecting ordinary consumers, at least that’s not how they have framed it publicly in the past.”

Beyond the companies handling the data, there are questions about whether consumers understand what they are agreeing to. The Tim Hortons app, in its user policies, states that when customers use it, they agree to its terms.

“Research shows that consumers are frequently unaware of the particulars they consent to when accepting a privacy policy,” Johanna Gunawan, an assistant professor of computer science and law at Maastricht University, told Al Jazeera.

Such policies are lengthy and often not conveyed in plain language, she said.

“The cognitive load to understand the full privacy implications of acceptance is frequently imbalanced against the relative ease or speed of providing agreement,” explained Gunawan.

Israeli military intelligence links

Questions about the app’s data practices do not end with what information is collected or whether users consent to sharing it. They also extend to the company receiving that data.

Forter’s founders – Michael Reitblat, Liron Damri and Alon Shemesh – are all alumni of the Israeli military’s Unit 8200, its signals intelligence and cyberwarfare division, The Times of Israel has reported. The company’s technology is enhanced by Israeli military intelligence, The Jerusalem Post reported in 2018.

Last year, Microsoft barred the Israeli military from some of its services following an investigation which found that Unit 8200 used its Azure cloud computing platform to store phone call data obtained through mass surveillance of Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

The division has also been associated with Lavender, the AI technology that Israel has created to target Palestinians during its genocidal war on Gaza.

While the ties are “concerning”, said CPJME’s Toney, he cautioned against speculating whether Forter uses data collected through the Tim Hortons app in a “nefarious” manner. There is no evidence of this, and he added that the Israeli firm appears to be well established.

On its website, Forter says it works on fraud prevention for many high-profile companies, ranging from eBay to Shein, Reebok and LG Electronics.

Al Jazeera was not able to confirm whether Forter still uses Israeli military intelligence or whether any data it holds is accessible to the Israeli government or military agencies.

Outdated privacy laws

This is not the first time Tim Hortons has landed in hot water over its handling of user data.

In 2022, Canadian federal and provincial privacy commissioners found that the company’s app had illegally tracked users’ locations through a third-party provider, even when the app was closed.

Tim Hortons faced no fines then because Canada’s privacy regulator cannot issue them, said OpenMedia’s Hatfield.

He said Canada’s privacy laws are insufficient and outdated.

“Our federal private-sector privacy law, PIPEDA, is more than 25 years old. Under it, a company can send your data to a service provider without asking you, as long as it says it remains ‘accountable’ for that data,” said Hatfield, referring to Canada’s Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act.

“In practice, Canadians often can’t find out who receives their data, which country it ends up in, or which foreign laws or governments might be able to reach it.”

He said companies should be telling their customers this directly and respecting their stated preferences for how their data is used.

Bill C-36, the government’s new proposed privacy legislation introduced in June this year, meanwhile, “would only partially help”, said the digital rights advocate.

“It would require a privacy impact assessment before data leaves Canada, and it would introduce real financial penalties,” said Hatfield. “But it still lets companies hand data to service providers without consent, and those providers would only be directly bound by its security and breach-reporting rules.”

More worryingly, he added, the bill places privacy enforcement under a new regulator, which will be required to consider factors beyond privacy, including Canada’s trade agreements, economic growth and the broader public interest, before launching an investigation into a privacy violation.

“In practice, this may mean that while privacy violations may be more clearly illegal once C-36 passes, the Canadian government could pressure the regulator to ignore violations associated with close trade partners,” said Hatfield.

Despite the results of its last investigation, CPJME is now calling for another inquiry by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada to look into the handling of consumer data by Tim Hortons, said Toney.

Al Jazeera contacted the privacy commissioner’s office about this but did not receive a response.

‘Off the hook’

Toney’s organisation has also filed a complaint with the CBC’s ombudsperson, citing violations in journalistic standards and practices for failing to disclose Forter’s identity in its own investigation.

“CBC’s reporting obscures the true scale of the privacy risk Tim Hortons has exposed its users to. CBC is letting Tim Hortons and Forter off the hook. Canadians deserve to understand the truth,” said Toney.

Maastricht University’s Gunawan said she also believes companies should take responsibility for the privacy and security practices of third-party technology providers.

“That’s simple transparency and due diligence,” she said.

Hatfield said: “Questions about a vendor’s ties to any foreign military or intelligence service are legitimate and deserve clear answers. The same standard should apply whether the vendor is American, Chinese, Israeli or Canadian.”

At minimum, said Hatfield, Tim Hortons should publicly name every third party that receives data from its app and explain why it sends that data. The company should also disclose where the data is stored, and who can access it.

“And frankly, it shouldn’t be giving our data to anyone when its business is selling coffee and doughnuts!”

entries.title: FIFA Under-17 World Cup 2026 gets under way in Qatar despite USA withdrawal
entries.summary: The 25-day tournament will feature 48 teams, with Dominican Republic replacing USA as FIFA plays down security concerns.
entries.content:
The 25-day tournament will feature 48 teams, with Dominican Republic replacing USA as FIFA plays down security concerns.

The FIFA Under-17 World Cup has kicked off in Qatar, with 48 teams participating in the global youth football competition despite the United States’ withdrawal over security concerns last week.

The tournament, which opened with two concurrent matches on Thursday, will be played in the 2022 World Cup host nation over the next 24 days after FIFA dismissed security concerns in the country.

“Everyone is safe in Doha,” FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in the Qatari capital last week.

US Soccer withdrew its national team citing safety concerns last Thursday, but the sport’s global governing body, which is hosting the tournament, said at the time that its plans remained unchanged.

Qatar has not been targeted by missiles since July as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran.

“The safety and security of all participants and fans remain paramount. As with all FIFA tournaments and events, we are in close contact with the relevant authorities and ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌are looking forward to the tournament kickoff in Qatar,” FIFA told Al Jazeera in a statement hours after the USA’s announcement.

“In recent months, Qatar has successfully hosted several international events,” it added.

Qatar hosted two major international tournaments in the past two weeks.

MotoGP’s Qatar Grand Prix was successfully held on November 8 and the FIP Padel World Cup 2026 ended on the same day.

The tournament will be hosted at the competition complex in Aspire Zone, Qatar’s central sporting hub.

The December 13 final will be played at the Ahmad bin Ali Stadium, which was a FIFA World Cup 2022 venue.

entries.title: Where Roots Lie: Surviving Child Grooming and Exploitation
entries.summary: Sosa, a survivor of trafficking and gang exploitation in the UK, returns to Nigeria to search for his missing mother.
entries.content:
Witness

Where Roots Lie: Surviving Child Grooming and Exploitation

Sosa, a survivor of trafficking and gang exploitation in the UK, returns to Nigeria to search for his missing mother.

Prominent United Kingdom anti-trafficking and anti-exploitation campaigner Sosa Henkoma returns to Nigeria to uncover the truth about his mother, who disappeared while trying to reach Europe years earlier. Born in Nigeria but raised in the UK, 27-year-old Sosa survived childhood abuse, gang violence and exploitation before transforming his life from teenage gang member to charismatic youth activist.

What begins as a search for his mother becomes a powerful exploration of identity, migration and belonging, as well as the wider forces that shaped both their lives.

Where Roots Lie is a documentary film by Samir Modi.

Published On 19 Nov 2026

entries.title: Mosque set on fire in Israel, politicians blame Netanyahu’s ‘incitement’
entries.summary: Knesset MPs call the incident 'a hate crime' while Hamas blames Israeli 'settler gangs'.
entries.content:
Knesset MPs call the incident ‘a hate crime’ while Hamas blames Israeli ‘settler gangs’.

Police are investigating after a mosque was set on fire in al-Dahi, a village in northern Israel where Palestinian citizens of Israel live.

The attack near the city of Afula on Thursday came after a car-ramming late on Wednesday targeted another city that is home to Palestinian citizens of Israel.

A slate of politicians have blamed the mosque attack on “incitement” by the camp of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

“An investigation has been opened into the suspected arson of a room in the lower part of a mosque in the village of al-Dahi and the spraying of graffiti on a nearby street,” police said in a statement.

“The Israel Police takes any attempt to harm religious symbols very seriously and will act decisively and without compromise to bring the suspects to justice,” they added.

The mosque’s imam, Khaled al-Zoubi, said he had seen “smoke and a fire” when he arrived for dawn prayer on Thursday.

“We came to the mosque, and there was smoke and fire burning from the bottom part of the mosque,” he said, explaining that the mosque has two floors.

“Three masked individuals came from the woods on the mountain we have here; they tried to enter the inside of the mosque, the first floor, but there was an iron gate there, so they couldn’t get in.

“They went down from this area, entered, and broke the window of the mosque’s ground floor, and they had an incendiary bottle with them; they threw it, of course, and burned the mosque from below,” he recounted.

Senior Hamas official Abdul Rahman Shadid said attackers set fire to the mosque early on Thursday and wrote racist slogans on its walls. Photos from the AFP news agency showed graffiti reading “revenge” scrawled on the walls of buildings near the mosque.

‘Extremist settler militias’

“Setting a mosque on fire is a heinous hate crime. This is not Jewish and it is not Israeli,” said Yair Lapid, a leading member of the anti-Netanyahu bloc.

“The rampant incitement against Arab Israelis must stop,” he wrote on X, pointing to Netanyahu’s right-wing camp.

Yair Golan, who heads the left-leaning Democrats party, described the incident as “Jewish terrorism”.

“It is the consequence of the campaign of incitement Netanyahu and his government are waging against Arab citizens of Israel,” he said.

The head of the Arab-majority Joint List, Youssef Jabareen, visited the village of al-Dahi on Thursday.

“We hold Netanyahu and his entire cabinet, and all the extremists with him, responsible for translating their dangerous incitement into reality through attacks on our people,” said Jabareen.

Mansour Abbas, a member of Israel’s Knesset and Ra’am chairman, also condemned the attack.

“A hate crime, an act of terror, and the desecration of a holy place. This is not an isolated incident, but a direct result of the far right’s incitement campaign against Arab citizens,” he said. “I call on Prime Minister Netanyahu – stop the incitement. Granting legitimacy to violence endangers human life.”

Hamas condemned the attack that it blamed on “settler gangs”.

The attack reflects “the scale of organised terrorism carried out by extremist settler militias under the protection of the right-wing occupation government,” Hamas official Shadid said.

He added that such attacks were intended to “displace our people and empty the land of its inhabitants” through killing, burning and intimidation.

The attack came shortly after Israeli police arrested a man suspected of carrying out a ramming attack in Kaf Qasim, another city where Palestinian citizens of Israel live, late on Wednesday.

Eight people were injured in that attack. A Palestinian civil society organisation said the suspect is an Israeli settler. Police also said they had opened an investigation.

entries.title: South Korean court orders retrial for ex-PM Han over martial law attempt
entries.summary: The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court's legal interpretation of insurrection.
entries.content:
The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court’s legal interpretation of insurrection.

South Korea’s Supreme Court has ⁠⁠overturned the 15-year prison sentence of former Prime ⁠⁠Minister Han Duck-soo for his role in the brief imposition of martial law two years ago, sending the case back ⁠⁠to a lower court.

A majority of justices found shortcomings in the lower court’s assessment of Han’s actions before former President Yoon Suk Yeol’s declaration, particularly his proposal to convene a Cabinet meeting that could have given legitimacy to the president’s decision.

The justices said it was difficult to establish whether Han had intended to undermine the Constitution, given the urgent circumstances at the time.

The special prosecution team for Han’s case said in a statement that they respect the ⁠⁠court’s ruling.

The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court’s legal interpretation.

In the aftermath of the imposition of martial law, former President Yoon was impeached and removed from office by the Constitutional Court in April 2025.

A presidential election two months later brought Lee Jae Myung to power.

Yoon’s 2024 decree plunged the country into chaos, but lasted only about six hours as opposition lawmakers scrambled to overturn the decision.

Han, 77, one of several top officials sentenced over the short-lived martial law bid, was handed a 23-year jail term in January for his involvement, which the court said threatened “the constitutional order” and amounted to insurrection.

An appeals court then reduced the sentence to 15 years in May, citing Han’s “more than 50 years as a public official prior to the martial law declaration”.

Han has denied wrongdoing in relation to ⁠⁠all charges except one for perjury. He said last year that while he regretted not being able to stop Yoon from declaring martial law, he “never agreed to it or tried to help”.

Yoon, meanwhile, has ⁠⁠denied wrongdoing and said he exercised his powers as president. He was convicted of insurrection in February and sentenced to life in ⁠⁠prison.

He has appealed and awaits that ruling, which ⁠⁠is scheduled for January.

entries.title: ‘Groundbreaking’ Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Five key takeaways
entries.summary: Leaders hailed the unprecedented meeting as historic, with discussions spanning nuclear risks to energy flows.
entries.content:
Leaders hailed the unprecedented trilateral summit as historic, with discussions spanning nuclear risks to energy flows.

The presidents of the United States, China and Russia have declared a shared intent to stabilise energy flows, prevent nuclear proliferation and find mechanisms to work more closely together, at an unprecedented summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday.

The meeting, held on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conclave, was the highlight of three days of intense diplomacy in the region, where leaders from multiple countries — including US President Donald Trump — had previously gathered in Manila for other summits.

Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired the summit with Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, after a series of bilateral meetings among the leaders.

At the end of a more than one-hour-long meeting, they released what they described as a “peace declaration”. They met at a time when multiple wars — including the US war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine — have taken a heavy toll on economies and people around the world.

Here are some key takeaways from their summit:

Landmark meeting, ‘peace declaration’

Trump said that the meeting was between “three of the world’s largest nations,” mentioning that the trio of countries also hold the planet’s three biggest nuclear arsenals. “We’re making history,” the US leader said in his opening remarks, referring to their trilateral summit.

The US president added that “too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” however, Trump noted, “No peace [was] ever forged by declining opportunities.”

All three leaders reiterated that it was up to them to protect the world.

China’s Xi said the countries should shed a “Cold War mentality” and become friends — something reiterated by Russia’s Putin, in his own words, adding that the three countries can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively.

After the meeting, the trio released a joint “peace declaration”.

Stable energy flows

Under the China-US-Russia “peace declaration”, the three countries have reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows, Chinese state media reported.

Global energy supplies have been on edge since the US attacked Iran in February this year, and Tehran closed down the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil supplies previously transited. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further compounded global energy woes.

But there appears to be no end to both wars — either by the US or Russia — and it remains unclear how the promise of stable energy flows will be realised given the different priorities of the three nations.

In fact, there was no reference to the war on Iran at the summit — other than Trump reiterating that Tehran cannot have a nuclear weapon. And a Kremlin spokesperson said that Ukraine was not even the “central topic” at the trilateral meeting, though it was a central part of Putin’s bilateral talks with Trump earlier. Trump also called on Xi to help out in resolving the war on Ukraine.

Nuclear talks

In a major statement before the trilateral meeting started, China’s Xi said, “Nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world.

“Nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought; every effort must be made to prevent it,” he added.

The thrust of that statement was also later adopted in the post-meeting joint declaration, with three countries pledging to hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation. The leaders also committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security at their trilateral meeting.

In his opening remarks at the meeting, the US president said that the “three countries are uniquely positioned to discuss nuclear weapons” — given they hold the biggest arsenals.

Trump also said Xi agreed with him that the Strait of Hormuz needs to stay open and that Iran must not be allowed to have nuclear weapons. Tehran has repeatedly said that its nuclear mission is for civilian purposes and that it holds no desire to build weapons.

The start of a G3?

As the US, Russia, and China sat down for the trilateral meeting to discuss a variety of issues, European leaders gathered nervously in Berlin, analysts say, at a meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.

The leaders of these three countries appeared to take it upon themselves to solve the conflicts and issues plaguing global economies.

Next month, President Trump is hosting the G20 Summit in Miami, Florida, and China’s Xi Jinping is almost certain to attend. But Russia too is a member of the G20.

President Putin has skipped recent summits of the grouping because of an International Criminal Court warrant against him for the Ukraine war, and because European members of the G20 have been clear that they do not want to share a room with him.

Trump, however, has invited Putin to attend the Miami G20. The US is not a part of the ICC, so it is under no obligation to arrest the Russian president.

“The discussion at the trilateral summit was very frank and helped the leaders to better understand one another,” Putin said after the meeting.

Is this the start of a G3? We shall know in the coming weeks.

Critique of the ICC

Among the many points in the “peace declaration” agreed upon by Trump, Xi, and Putin in Shenzhen was a pointed critique of the International Criminal Court.

The three leaders demanded that the ICC and “similar institutions” not “abuse their positions”.

What is it about the ICC that upsets all three powers — none of whom are members of the court?

  • United States: The US has long had an adversarial relationship with the ICC, but those ties have grown especially tense in recent years after the court began investigating allegations of abuse by US soldiers in Afghanistan. The court’s warrant for the arrest of Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu on charges of having committed war crimes in Gaza caused a further rupture, and the US has now publicly, as part of official policy, made the dismemberment of the ICC a goal. It has imposed sanctions against the institutions and its officials.
  • Russia: Like the US, Russia has never trusted the ICC. But after the ICC issued an arrest warrant against President Putin on charges related to the Russian war on Ukraine, Moscow has become even more fiercely opposed to the UN court and its way of functioning.
  • China: There have been times in previous years when China — while never endorsing the court — has been lukewarm to it. But the spate of arrest warrants against leaders of sovereign nations, including Philippines ex-President Rodrigo Duterte, turned Beijing into a strident critic. The ICC has also received petitions from activists accusing China of committing genocide against the Uighur community in Xinjiang — an allegation Beijing rejects.
